text: Lesson two set a cost and latency budget for Northbeam's current traffic. This lesson asks the next question a Staff or Principal engineer owns: current traffic isn't the traffic that matters -- future traffic is. Infrastructure built to exactly fit today's load is already behind by the time it ships.

Northbeam's assistant currently handles two million requests a day, and it's growing at a steady fifteen percent month over month as more internal teams and customers adopt it. Its current infrastructure was sized to comfortably handle up to five million requests a day. Project that growth rate forward, and the math says Northbeam hits that ceiling in just seven months. That's a very different, far more useful fact than 'we're currently at two million and comfortable' -- the comfortable-sounding current state is not the number that should drive the infrastructure roadmap.

Knowing it's month seven isn't itself the actionable number -- how long the fix takes to actually implement is. If migrating to a higher-capacity vector database tier, renegotiating API rate limits, or re-architecting a bottlenecked component takes three months of real engineering work, that work needs to start by month four, not month seven. A capacity plan that only tracks when the ceiling hits, and not how much lead time the fix needs, reliably produces last-minute scrambles even when the forecast itself was completely accurate.

And capacity planning isn't just 'always build more headroom.' Extra infrastructure capacity has a real, ongoing cost, so the actual decision is a tradeoff between how much headroom is worth paying for and how much risk of a capacity-driven outage is tolerable. A single internal tool might reasonably tolerate occasional degraded performance to control cost. A paid, customer-facing product, where an outage directly costs revenue and trust, usually justifies far more conservative headroom, even at higher cost. There's no universal right answer -- it's a business decision informed by engineering facts, which is exactly why this is Staff and Principal-level work.
Next, we design to survive the failures lesson one said were guaranteed to happen -- multi-region and high-availability design for AI systems.
